stages.name: Monopsony power and wage intervention
stages.title: Monopsony power and wage intervention
stages.sub: See why a dominant employer can hold wages down, and why that justifies government intervention.

steps.q: A mining town has one large mine and no other employer for miles. If a miner does not like the wage, what can they realistically do about it?
steps.right: Very little, there is nowhere else to go
steps.wrong: Easily move to another local employer
steps.hint: Think about how many employers are actually available to these workers.

steps.q: Because miners have no other employer to turn to, can the mine offer a lower wage than it would if it had to compete with other employers for workers?
steps.right: Yes, it can push the wage down
steps.wrong: No, it must still pay the going rate
steps.hint: If workers cannot leave for a better-paying rival, what stops the firm cutting the wage?

steps.q: Given it is the sole buyer of labour and can set the wage below what a competitive market would pay, what does this firm hold over the labour market?
steps.right: Power to set wages below the competitive level
steps.wrong: Power only to set the price of its product
steps.hint: This is about buying labour, not selling output.

steps.q: If workers are being paid less than they would earn in a competitive market, purely because they have no alternative employer, should the government step in, for example with a minimum wage?
steps.right: Yes, to push the wage back up towards the competitive level
steps.wrong: No, the wage was freely agreed so it must be fair
steps.hint: Think about why the low wage exists here: is it because workers freely chose it, or because they had no choice?
